question: In which year did Babur defeat Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1526.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The First Battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526 between Babur and the Delhi Sultan Ibrahim Lodi, the last ruler of the Lodi dynasty (पानीपत का प्रथम युद्ध — बाबर बनाम इब्राहिम लोदी, 1526)

 

• Babur had been invited to India by Daulat Khan Lodi and Alam Khan Lodi, with Rana Sanga also reported among those who sought his help.

 

• Babur's success rested on his disciplined cavalry and his field artillery, which Ibrahim Lodi's larger army could not match.

 

• The victory ended the Delhi Sultanate and began the Mughal dynasty, whose first capital was Agra.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gunpowder had reached India earlier, but Panipat I is remembered as the first major battle where it decided the outcome.

 

• Babur was born in Fergana on 14 February 1483 and became its ruler at the age of 12 in 1494.

 

• He died in 1530 and was first buried at Aram Bagh in Agra before reburial at Kabul.

 

• Panipat was the site of three famous battles: 1526, 1556 and 1761.

 

NOTE

 

• 1519 (Option 1): 1519 is the year of Babur's first expedition into India, when he attacked Bajaur and Bhira; he was still far from reaching Delhi and Ibrahim Lodi was not confronted then.

 

• 1527 (Option 3): 1527 is the year of the Battle of Khanwa against Rana Sanga of Mewar, fought a year after Panipat to remove the Rajput threat to his new kingdom.

 

• 1529 (Option 4): 1529 is the year of the Battle of Ghaghra against the Afghans under Mahmud Lodi and Sher Khan, which secured eastern India for Babur.

question: Babur is credited with using a gun for the first time in India during his attack on:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bajaur (Bhira).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In 1519, in his first expedition into India, Babur attacked Bajaur (Bhira) in Punjab and used a gun there for the first time (बाजौर/भीरा — 1519 में बाबर का भारत पर पहला आक्रमण)

 

• Babur launched about four expeditions between 1519 and 1523 before the final march that led to Panipat.

 

• After these raids he took Lahore easily by defeating its governor Daulat Khan Lodi, and then marched on Delhi against Ibrahim Lodi.

 

• The Bajaur success showed him the value of firearms combined with mobile cavalry, a mix he perfected at Panipat in 1526.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gunpowder artillery was used on a large scale in India at Panipat I (1526), though Babur did not introduce gunpowder itself.

 

• Babur's Ottoman-style tactics were the tulughma (flanking movement) and the arrangement of carts tied together with ropes (araba).

 

• Mustafa Rumi is remembered as his famed Ottoman gunner.

 

• Bhira lay in the Salt Range region of Punjab, now in Pakistan.

 

NOTE

 

• Lahore (Option 2): Lahore fell to Babur later, when he advanced against Daulat Khan Lodi on the way to Delhi; it was an occupation without a notable gun battle and not the first use of a gun.

 

• Chanderi (Option 3): Chanderi in Malwa was attacked in 1528 against the Rajput chief Medini Rai, long after Babur had first employed guns at Bajaur.

 

• Kalinjar (Option 4): Kalinjar is associated with Sher Shah Suri, who died there in 1545 when a gun-fired shell exploded during the siege, and has no link with Babur's first use of guns.

question: The Battle of Ghaghra (1529) was notable because it was the first time in Indian history that:
option_2: The navy and the army fought together
option_4: A Rajput army defeated a Mughal force
solution_text:
The correct answer is The navy and the army fought together.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• At the Battle of Ghaghra (1529) Babur fought the Afghans led by Mahmud Lodi and Sher Khan, and it was the first time the navy and army fought together (घाघरा का युद्ध — नौसेना और थलसेना का संयुक्त प्रयोग)

 

• The victory ended the Afghan challenge in eastern India and Bihar for the time being, completing Babur's conquests.

 

• It was the last major battle of his life; he died in 1530, just a year later.

 

• Babur's four main Indian battles were Panipat (1526), Khanwa (1527), Chanderi (1528) and Ghaghra (1529).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sher Khan, who fought here against Babur, later defeated Humayun at Chausa and Bilgram and founded the Suri dynasty.

 

• The Battle of Khanwa (1527) had earlier removed Rana Sanga, the main Rajput rival.

 

• Babur authored about these campaigns in his Turkish memoir, the Tuzuk-i-Baburi.

 

• The Ghaghra river joins the Ganga in Bihar, where Babur's boats and cannon supported his land troops, and the victory kept eastern India under Mughal control.

 

NOTE

 

• Elephants were used against cavalry (Option 1): Elephants were a standard feature of Indian warfare for centuries and were used by Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat, so their use was no novelty in 1529 and Ghaghra is not known for it.

 

• Gunpowder was used in battle (Option 3): Gunpowder was seen in Indian battles at Panipat in 1526, three years before Ghaghra, so Ghaghra was not the first occasion for this distinction.

 

• A Rajput army defeated a Mughal force (Option 4): Babur won at Ghaghra against the Afghans; Rajputs were fought at Khanwa and Chanderi in 1527-28 and no Rajput victory over Babur's forces occurred at Ghaghra.

question:
Match the battles with the opponents of Babur.

Column A: (a) Panipat I (b) Khanwa (c) Chanderi (d) Ghaghra

Column B: (i) Medini Rai (ii) Afghans under Mahmud Lodi and Sher Khan (iii) Ibrahim Lodi (iv) Rana Sanga
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Panipat I (1526) was fought against Ibrahim Lodi, so (a) matches (iii) (पानीपत प्रथम — इब्राहिम लोदी)

 

• Khanwa (1527) was fought against Rana Sanga of Mewar, who had gathered a huge Rajput confederacy, so (b) matches (iv).

 

• Chanderi (1528), in the Malwa region, was fought against the Rajput chief Medini Rai, so (c) matches (i).

 

• Ghaghra (1529) was fought against the Afghans led by Mahmud Lodi and Sher Khan, so (d) matches (ii).

 

• Taken together, the four contests trace Babur's rise: Panipat gave him Delhi and Agra, Khanwa broke Rajput power, Chanderi opened Malwa and Ghaghra neutralised the Afghans of the east.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Babur's victory at Khanwa earned him the title Ghazi.

 

• Babur won all four battles, each time through superior tactics and artillery.

 

• Rana Sanga died in 1528, a year after Khanwa.

 

• These four battles are the standard Babur sequence repeated in the chapter's battle table.

 

• Babur's army used cannon, matchlock men, and mobile cavalry, which gave him a technological edge over Indian armies of the early sixteenth century.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii (Option 1): This swaps Panipat I with Khanwa, giving Ibrahim Lodi to Khanwa and Rana Sanga to Panipat; in fact Sanga was beaten in 1527 while Ibrahim Lodi died at Panipat in 1526.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii (Option 2): This pairs Khanwa with Medini Rai and Chanderi with Rana Sanga, reversing two correct matches; Medini Rai held Chanderi in Malwa and Sanga was the Khanwa opponent.

 

• a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii (Option 3): This gives Panipat I to the Afghans and Ghaghra to Ibrahim Lodi, which is wrong because Ibrahim Lodi was killed in 1526 and the Afghans were met only in 1529.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Baburnama):

1. It was written in Turkish.

2. Its Persian translation was done by Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana during Akbar's reign.

3. It is the autobiography of Humayun.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Tuzuk-i-Baburi was composed in Turkish (Chagatai), Babur's mother tongue (बाबरनामा — बाबर की आत्मकथा, तुर्की भाषा में)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana, son of Bairam Khan and a Navratna of Akbar, translated it into Persian.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: it is the autobiography of Babur himself; it is regarded as the first autobiography of the Mughal era.

 

• Humayun's life was recorded separately in the Humayunama by his sister Gulbadan Begum.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Babur also introduced the Gaz-i-Babari as a measure of land length.

 

• Jahangir later authored his own memoir, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, in Persian.

 

• The Baburnama describes the flora, fauna and politics of Hindustan with strong personal observation.

 

• Khan-i-Khana was the title given to Bairam Khan and later passed to his son Abdul Rahim.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 only (Option 1): Statement 1 alone is incomplete because the Persian translation by Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana is also a correct fact, so selecting only the first statement misses a true one.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Pairing the second claim with the third fails, because attributing the Baburnama to Humayun is wrong; Humayun's life is covered by the Humayunama of Gulbadan Begum, and Babur composed his own memoir.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Including all three fails since statement 3 is false; the Tuzuk-i-Baburi is Babur's own memoir and not the autobiography of Humayun.

question: All of the following were built by Babur EXCEPT:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Purana Qila at Delhi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Purana Qila on the Yamuna bank near Delhi was built by Sher Shah Suri, with red sandstone and white marble, and is not Babur's work (पुराना किला — शेरशाह सूरी द्वारा निर्मित)

 

• Babur built the Kabuli Bagh mosque at Panipat in 1526 to mark his victory over Ibrahim Lodi.

 

• He laid out the Aram Bagh garden in Agra, where he was first buried before being shifted to Kabul.

 

• The Babri Mosque at Ayodhya (1527-28) was built by his general Mir Baqi under his command.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sher Shah's Delhi city, Sher Garh, is counted as the sixth city of Delhi.

 

• Humayun founded Din Panah in Delhi, which Sher Shah later partly rebuilt.

 

• Babur's gardens followed the Persian charbagh layout.

 

• Another Babur-linked mosque is the Jami Masjid at Sambhal.

 

• Babur's rule in India lasted only four years, 1526 to 1530, yet he laid down the foundation of a dynasty that ruled for more than three hundred years.

 

NOTE

 

• Kabuli Bagh Mosque at Panipat (Option 2): The Kabuli Bagh mosque in Panipat dates to 1526 and is a genuine Babur construction, so it cannot be the exception asked for in this question.

 

• Aram Bagh at Agra (Option 3): Aram Bagh at Agra was laid out under Babur and served as his first burial site, so this garden is also properly attributed to him.

 

• Babri Mosque at Ayodhya (Option 4): The Babri Mosque built at Ayodhya in 1527-28 is credited to Mir Baqi, Babur's commander, and so it falls among the structures linked with his reign.

question: In the Battle of Chausa (1539), Humayun was defeated by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sher Khan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• At Chausa (1539) Humayun was defeated by the Afghan chief Sher Khan, who then captured Gaur and took the title Sher Shah (चौसा का युद्ध, 1539 — हुमायूँ बनाम शेर खाँ)

 

• Humayun escaped from the battlefield by crossing the Ganga, and the defeat shattered the confidence of his army.

 

• After Chausa he went to Agra to seek help from his brothers, who refused to cooperate.

 

• He therefore had to face Sher Shah alone at Bilgram (Kanauj) in 1540, lost again and went into exile for about 15 years.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• After Chausa Sher Khan also assumed the title Sultan-i-Adil.

 

• The Suri dynasty ruled from 1540 to 1555.

 

• Humayun's brothers were Kamran, Askari and Hindal.

 

• Humayun is called fortunate by name but was the most unfortunate of the Mughal rulers.

 

• After Chausa the Afghans resumed control of North India, and Suri rule continued until 1555, when Humayun took the throne back.

 

NOTE

 

• Sikandar Sur (Option 1): Sikandar Sur was beaten by Humayun at Sirhind in 1555, when the Mughal emperor regained his throne, so he was the loser and not the winner at Chausa.

 

• Hemu (Option 2): Hemu fought Akbar's forces at the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556, which happened after Humayun's death, so he cannot be linked with the 1539 encounter.

 

• Mahmud Lodi (Option 4): Mahmud Lodi joined the Afghan opposition to Babur at Ghaghra in 1529, a decade before Chausa, and he did not defeat Humayun.

question: Akbar was born in 1542 at the palace of Amarkot, where Humayun had taken shelter with:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rana Prasad.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Akbar was born on 15 October 1542 at Amarkot in Sindh, whose ruler Rana Prasad gave shelter to the exiled Humayun (अमरकोट — अकबर का जन्मस्थान, राणा प्रसाद का राज्य)

 

• Humayun's wife Hamida Banu Begum, whom he had married in 1541 in the desert of Sindh, was Akbar's mother.

 

• Humayun then left India and lived on the generosity of the king of Persia, who lent him a force of about 14,000 men.

 

• With that help he later captured Kabul and finally defeated the Suris to regain Delhi in 1555.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Akbar was named Jalaluddin Muhammad (also recorded as Badruddin).

 

• He was crowned at Kalanaur in Punjab in 1556 after Humayun's death.

 

• Humayun blinded his brother Kamran in 1553 and sent him to Mecca, where Kamran died in 1557.

 

• Amarkot is in Sindh, now in Pakistan.

 

• Humayun's tomb at Delhi was begun about nine years after his death in 1556, and Akbar supervised the completion of the work.

 

NOTE

 

• Raja Bharmal (Option 1): Raja Bharmal of Amber was the Rajput chief whose daughter Akbar married later, and he had no connection with Humayun's exile shelter at Amarkot.

 

• Maldeo Rathore (Option 2): Maldeo Rathore was the Marwar ruler of that period and is not the host at Amarkot; the notes name Rana Prasad as the ruler who sheltered Humayun's family.

 

• Medini Rai (Option 3): Medini Rai was the Rajput chief of Chanderi whom Babur defeated in 1528, and he was never connected with the birth of Akbar.

question:
Assertion (A): Humayun's Tomb in Delhi is regarded as the precursor of the Taj Mahal.

Reason (R): It introduced the Charbagh garden layout and a double-domed mausoleum style in the Indian subcontinent.
option_1: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Humayun's Tomb was built by his wife Haji Begum (Bega Begum), designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and finished by Akbar, so the assertion is true (हुमायूँ का मकबरा — ताजमहल का पूर्वगामी)

 

• It was the first garden tomb of the subcontinent and introduced the Charbagh layout, so the reason is also true.

 

• The Taj Mahal borrowed exactly these elements, a Charbagh garden and a double-dome on a high platform, which is why the reason explains the assertion.

 

• Both therefore hold good and R is the right explanation of A.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Humayun's biography, the Humayunama, was written by his sister Gulbadan Begum.

 

• Humayun's tomb is in Delhi near the Yamuna, and Humayun died in 1556 after falling from the stairs of his library, the Sher Mandal.

 

• The Taj Mahal was constructed between 1631 and 1653 under Shah Jahan.

 

• Akbar's Sikandra tomb and Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb are other major Mughal tombs.

 

NOTE

 

• A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): The second option accepts both statements as true, which is right, but wrongly denies the link: the Charbagh plan and double dome are precisely the features carried into the Taj Mahal.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): The third option calls the reason false, but the Charbagh garden layout and the double-domed mausoleum style are well-documented features of Humayun's Tomb, so R is true.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): The fourth option calls the assertion false, yet standard accounts treat Humayun's Tomb as the model that inspired the design of the Taj Mahal at Agra.

question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:

1. Battle of Chausa

2. Battle of Sirhind

3. Battle of Bilgram (Kanauj)

4. Second Battle of Panipat
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1-3-2-4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chausa was fought in 1539, where Sher Khan defeated Humayun and became Sher Shah (चौसा 1539 → बिलग्राम 1540 → सरहिंद 1555 → पानीपत द्वितीय 1556)

 

• Bilgram (Kanauj) followed in 1540, forcing Humayun into exile for about 15 years.

 

• Sirhind (1555) saw Humayun defeat Sikandar Sur and regain the throne of Delhi.

 

• The Second Battle of Panipat came in 1556, when Akbar's army under Bairam Khan defeated Hemu.

 

• Putting the sequence together shows a clear arc: Humayun's two defeats within a year (1539, 1540) cost him the throne, and his comeback at Sirhind in 1555 was cut short when he died within months.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Humayun died in 1556, a few months after returning to Delhi.

 

• The Suris ruled from 1540 to 1555.

 

• Sikandar Sur was the last Suri ruler.

 

• Humayun's second coronation is dated to 1555 after the Sirhind victory.

 

• Humayun's reconquest was helped by Persian soldiers and by divisions among the Afghan nobles after Islam Shah's death.

 

NOTE

 

• 3-1-2-4 (Option 1): This order places Bilgram before Chausa, but Chausa (1539) clearly preceded Bilgram (1540); Humayun's defeat at Chausa left him too weak and led directly to the later battle.

 

• 1-2-3-4 (Option 2): This puts Sirhind before Bilgram, which is impossible since Humayun's recovery at Sirhind in 1555 occurred after his loss and 15-year exile that followed Bilgram in 1540.

 

• 1-3-4-2 (Option 3): This places Panipat II ahead of Sirhind, although Akbar fought Hemu in 1556, after Humayun had already recovered Delhi in 1555 and died.

question: Humayun's biography, the 'Humayunama', was written by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gulbadan Begum.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Humayunama was written by Gulbadan Begum, daughter of Babur and sister of Humayun (हुमायूँनामा — गुलबदन बेगम द्वारा रचित)

 

• It gives an intimate account of Babur's and Humayun's reigns from a woman of the royal household.

 

• Gulbadan authored it at the request of Akbar, who wished to have a record of his father's life for Abul Fazal's Akbar Nama.

 

• She is one of the earliest women authors of the Mughal court.

 

• Because Gulbadan was an eyewitness to the household of both rulers, the book is valued as a rare account of Mughal domestic and political life from a woman's perspective.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Haji Begum built Humayun's tomb in Delhi.

 

• Abul Fazal authored the Akbar Nama, whose third volume is the Ain-i-Akbari.

 

• Hamida Banu Begum was Humayun's wife and Akbar's mother.

 

• Humayun died in 1556 after a fall from the stairs of the Sher Mandal.

 

• Gulbadan Begum was also an aunt of Akbar and travelled to Mecca on pilgrimage in the 1570s.

 

NOTE

 

• Abul Fazal (Option 1): Abul Fazal was Akbar's chief advisor and authored the three-volume Akbar Nama in Persian; he is not the author of the Humayunama, though his work covers Humayun briefly as an ancestor.

 

• Haji Begum (Option 3): Haji Begum, also called Bega Begum, is known as the builder of Humayun's tomb in Delhi, not as an author of any biography.

 

• Hamida Banu Begum (Option 4): Hamida Banu Begum was Humayun's wife whom he married in 1541 and the mother of Akbar; no literary work on Humayun is credited to her.

question: Sher Khan received his title 'Sher' from Bahar Khan Lohani, the ruler of Bihar, because he:
option_4: saved the ruler's life from a tiger
solution_text:
The correct answer is saved the ruler's life from a tiger.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bahar Khan Lohani, an Afghan ruler of Bihar, gave the title Sher Khan because he saved his life from a tiger (शेर खाँ — बिहार के बहार खाँ लोहानी द्वारा बाघ से रक्षा पर दी गई उपाधि)

 

• The name Sher means tiger, so the title was a recognition of personal bravery before his rise to power.

 

• After the victory at Chausa (1539) he assumed the higher title Sher Shah, and later also Sultan-i-Adil.

 

• He founded the Suri dynasty after beating Humayun at Bilgram in 1540.

 

• The tiger incident happened while Sher Khan served the Afghan chief of Bihar, and it marks the beginning of the career that took him from a jagirdar's son to ruler of Delhi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sher Shah's original name was Farid.

 

• He ruled from 1540 to 1545 and built the Purana Qila in Delhi.

 

• His tomb at Sasaram in Bihar is a fine example of Afghan architecture.

 

• He died while besieging Kalinjar.

 

• The Sur dynasty founded by Sher Shah ruled North India for about fifteen years from 1540 to 1555 with Sasaram, Bihar as the family home.

 

NOTE

 

• won the Battle of Chausa (Option 1): Winning at Chausa came years after the title Sher Khan was already in use; that victory led him to adopt the royal style Sher Shah rather than earning the original title.

 

• conquered Gaur (Option 2): Conquering Gaur happened after Chausa, when he captured it and assumed higher titles; the earlier honorific from Bahar Khan Lohani had nothing to do with that conquest.

 

• defeated Humayun at Bilgram (Option 3): Bilgram (1540) was his second victory over Humayun and established his rule in Delhi, far later than the incident with the tiger that gave him his first title.

question:
Match the ministers in Sher Shah's administration with their charges.

Column A: (a) Diwan-i-Wizarat (b) Diwan-i-Ariz (c) Diwan-i-Rasalat (d) Diwan-i-Insha

Column B: (i) Foreign ministry (ii) Communication (iii) Revenue and Finance (iv) Defence
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Diwan-i-Wizarat (the Wazir) looked after revenue and finance, so (a) matches (iii) (शेरशाह के चार मंत्री — वजारत, आरिज, रसालत, इंशा)

 

• Diwan-i-Ariz headed the defence department, matching (b) with (iv).

 

• Diwan-i-Rasalat was the foreign ministry, matching (c) with (i).

 

• Diwan-i-Insha handled communication, matching (d) with (ii).

 

• The offices were separate heads of government under Sher Shah, who personally supervised them; the arrangement of specialised departments was later adopted by Akbar and other Mughal rulers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sher Shah's system was later used as a blueprint for Akbar's administration.

 

• Sher Shah ruled between 1540 and 1545.

 

• His mausoleum stands at Sasaram in Bihar.

 

• Mughal administration kept the Diwan for revenue and the Mir Bakhshi for the army.

 

• Sher Shah also built roads with sarais, introduced the silver rupee and dam coins, and the Grand Trunk Road from Sonargaon to Peshawar was repaired and extended.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii (Option 1): This swaps Wizarat and Ariz, giving finance to the defence ministry; Diwan-i-Wizarat was the revenue office headed by the Wazir while Diwan-i-Ariz was military in function.

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 3): This interchanges the last two pairs, giving Rasalat communication and Insha foreign affairs, which reverses the actual duties of those two offices.

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-iii, d-ii (Option 4): This gives Wizarat foreign affairs and Rasalat finance, while keeping Insha as communication; revenue and foreign duties are both misplaced, so the combination fails.

question: Sher Shah Suri died in 1545 while besieging the fort of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kalinjar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sher Shah died in 1545 during the siege of Kalinjar fort when a shell fired by artillery burst accidentally (कालिंजर का दुर्ग — शेरशाह की मृत्यु 1545)

 

• His tomb stands on an artificial lake at Sasaram in Bihar.

 

• After him the Suri successors ruled until 1555, when Humayun reconquered India.

 

• The last Suri ruler was Sikandar Suri, defeated at Sirhind.

 

• The accident came while Sher Shah was directing the assault on the Chandela fort in Bundelkhand, so his short but energetic reign ended in the midst of a campaign.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sher Shah's short reign left Purana Qila and Sher Garh as monuments in Delhi.

 

• Sher Garh is counted as the sixth city of Delhi.

 

• He ruled from 1540 to 1545.

 

• Islam Shah succeeded him as the next Suri ruler.

 

• Sher Shah's Purana Qila and its Qila-i-Kuhna mosque stand near the Yamuna in Delhi, and his tomb at Sasaram is a fine example of Afghan architecture.

 

NOTE

 

• Chittor (Option 2): Chittor was captured by Akbar in 1567 after a long siege against Uday Singh of the Sisodia dynasty, so it has no connection with the death of Sher Shah.

 

• Ranthambore (Option 3): Ranthambore fell to Akbar in 1569 and is a well-known Rajasthan fort; Sher Shah's final siege was elsewhere in Bundelkhand, not at this fort.

 

• Gwalior (Option 4): Gwalior was associated with Tansen's Sufi teacher Shaikh Muhammad Ghaus and with later Mughal conquests; Sher Shah did not die at its walls.

question: Akbar's regent from 1556 to 1560, who was given the title Khan-i-Khana, was:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bairam Khan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bairam Khan acted as regent of the young Akbar from 1556 to 1560 and served as his wazir; he held the title Khan-i-Khana (बैरम खाँ — अकबर का संरक्षक, खान-ए-खाना)

 

• Akbar was crowned at Kalanaur in Punjab in 1556, soon after Humayun's death, when he was still a boy.

 

• Bairam Khan became arrogant and harsh, so Akbar asked him to go on a pilgrimage to Mecca.

 

• On the way he was killed by Afghan tribesmen after rebelling in the Battle of Tilwara against Akbar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• His son Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana became one of the Navratna of Akbar.

 

• Bairam Khan led Akbar's forces against Hemu at Panipat II in 1556.

 

• Akbar was born at Amarkot to Humayun and Hamida Banu Begum.

 

• Akbar took full control of the empire after 1560.

 

• After 1560 Akbar governed with ministers of his own choice, and the experience of the regency helped him avoid dependence on a single powerful noble.

 

NOTE

 

• Todar Mal (Option 1): Todar Mal was Akbar's finance minister and revenue expert who developed the Zabti system, and he never served as regent during the minority.

 

• Adham Khan (Option 2): Adham Khan fought in the Malwa campaign of 1561 against Baz Bahadur on Akbar's side, but he was a military commander and not the regent of the empire.

 

• Man Singh (Option 3): Man Singh of Amber led the Mughal army at Haldighati in 1576, which was after Akbar began ruling independently, so he was not involved in the regency.

question: The Second Battle of Panipat (5 November 1556) was fought between Akbar's forces and:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hemu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the Second Battle of Panipat (1556), Akbar, acting through Bairam Khan, defeated the Afghan general Hemu (पानीपत का द्वितीय युद्ध — अकबर बनाम हेमू)

 

• Hemu was almost victorious, but an arrow pierced his eye and he fell unconscious; his army fled and the Mughal victory became decisive.

 

• The battle restored Mughal power in North India, which had been shaken after Humayun's death earlier that year.

 

• It came only a few months after Akbar's coronation at Kalanaur.

 

• Hemu had captured Delhi weeks earlier, so the quick counter-move led by Bairam Khan shows how a near-lost situation was turned into a decisive Mughal win.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hemu had earlier occupied Delhi and Agra after Humayun's death.

 

• Panipat has seen three decisive battles, in 1526, 1556 and 1761.

 

• The first battle in 1526 was won by Babur against Ibrahim Lodi.

 

• Bairam Khan was the key commander on the Mughal side.

 

• The Mughal victory at the plain of Panipat in 1556 is called the second of three major battles fought at the same place.

 

NOTE

 

• Sikandar Sur (Option 2): Sikandar Sur, the last Suri ruler, was defeated by Humayun at Sirhind in 1555, so he was not the enemy of Akbar at Panipat in 1556.

 

• Rana Pratap (Option 3): Rana Pratap fought Akbar's army only at Haldighati in 1576, twenty years after Panipat II, and he held no role at the 1556 battle.

 

• Baz Bahadur (Option 4): Baz Bahadur of Malwa was defeated in 1561 by Adham Khan on Akbar's behalf, which was a separate campaign and not the engagement at Panipat in 1556.

question: Akbar's marriage with the daughter of Raja Bharmal of Amber was a turning point in Mughal history because it:
option_1: Ended the Rajput resistance of Mewar
option_2: Led to the abolition of the mansabdari system
option_3: Began a lasting alliance with Rajput rulers who rose to high posts in the empire
option_4: Forced the Rajputs to accept Islam
solution_text:
The correct answer is Began a lasting alliance with Rajput rulers who rose to high posts in the empire.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Akbar's marriage to a Rajput princess, the daughter of Raja Bharmal, began a lasting alliance with the Rajputs (राजा भारमल की पुत्री से विवाह — राजपूत नीति का आरंभ)

 

• The Rajputs served the Mughals for four generations, and many rose to be senior generals, such as Raja Bhagwan Das and Raja Man Singh.

 

• One by one the Rajput states accepted Akbar's authority, while the Ranas of Mewar kept defying him.

 

• The Rajput policy went together with a broad religious toleration, including the abolition of the pilgrim tax and the jiziya.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Man Singh commanded the Mughal army at Haldighati in 1576.

 

• Bhagwan Das succeeded Raja Bharmal as the ruler of Amber and was among the first Rajputs to hold a high mansab.

 

• The Sisodias of Mewar were honoured by Jahangir after their final submission.

 

• The marriage took place in the early years of Akbar's reign.

 

• Akbar's Rajput policy brought a stable army, wide support in Rajasthan and a body of loyal Hindu generals to the empire.

 

NOTE

 

• Ended the Rajput resistance of Mewar (Option 1): Mewar continued to resist for a long time and only submitted under Jahangir, so the marriage did not end Mewar's opposition and the statement is inaccurate.

 

• Led to the abolition of the mansabdari system (Option 2): The mansabdari system was a ranking arrangement that Akbar developed and it remained in force throughout the Mughal period; the Rajput alliance did not cause its abolition.

 

• Forced the Rajputs to accept Islam (Option 4): Akbar followed a policy of religious toleration and abolished forced conversion of prisoners of war, so the alliance was not accompanied by any compulsion on Rajputs to accept Islam.

question: The Mughal army at the Battle of Haldighati (1576) was commanded by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Raja Man Singh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• At Haldighati (18 June 1576) Maharana Pratap of Mewar fought the Mughal forces under Raja Man Singh, Akbar's chief general (हल्दीघाटी — महाराणा प्रताप बनाम मान सिंह, 1576)

 

• The battle was inconclusive: Maharana Pratap did not die, though he lost the field.

 

• Mewar's Sisodias stubbornly refused Mughal suzerainty and continued resistance in the hills.

 

• Man Singh was one of the Navratna and held a senior place in Akbar's administration.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pratap's famous horse Chetak is remembered from this battle.

 

• The Sisodias were finally defeated in Jahangir's reign and treated honourably, with their lands returned.

 

• Chittor had earlier fallen to Akbar in 1567.

 

• Man Singh served Akbar in Kabul, Bengal and Orissa as well.

 

• The Haldighati pass lies in the Aravalli range near Udaipur, and Pratap continued guerrilla warfare for the remainder of his life, recovering most of Mewar except Chittor.

 

NOTE

 

• Todar Mal (Option 1): Todar Mal was Akbar's revenue minister who worked on the Zabti system, and he did not lead the Mughal troops against Mewar in 1576.

 

• Bairam Khan (Option 2): Bairam Khan was Akbar's regent who died in 1561 on the way to Mecca, so he was dead fifteen years before the battle took place.

 

• Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana (Option 3): Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana was a poet-general and a Navratna, known for translations and for later campaigns, but Man Singh and not he led the army at Haldighati.

question: Rani Durgawati of Gondwana fought against Akbar's general in the battle of Garha Katanga (1564). The general was:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Asaf Khan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In 1564 the Mughal general Asaf Khan invaded Gondwana (Garha-Katanga), where Rani Durgawati fought him bravely (गढ़ कटंगा, 1564 — रानी दुर्गावती बनाम आसफ खाँ)

 

• Asaf Khan fought on behalf of Akbar, who sought to extend his control over central India.

 

• Durgawati was the widow of the Gond king Dalpat Shah and ruled for her young son.

 

• Mughal power thus expanded into the Narmada region and central India.

 

• The defeat of Rani Durgawati, who died fighting rather than surrender, is remembered as a notable act of resistance by a woman ruler against the expanding Mughal state.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gondwana's Rani Durgawati was a Chandela Rajput princess by birth.

 

• Adham Khan's Malwa campaign of 1561 against Baz Bahadur was a different expedition.

 

• In 1567 Akbar captured Chittor from Uday Singh.

 

• In 1572 Akbar annexed Gujarat.

 

• The Gond kingdom lay near present Jabalpur, and the Rani's fort at Singaurgarh and the Narmada region saw the final fighting.

 

NOTE

 

• Adham Khan (Option 1): Adham Khan led the 1561 attack on Malwa against Baz Bahadur and later took the Chunar fort, and he had no part in the Gondwana campaign.

 

• Man Singh (Option 3): Man Singh won fame at Haldighati in 1576 and in other later campaigns, but he did not lead the 1564 expedition against Gondwana.

 

• Bairam Khan (Option 4): Bairam Khan had already been removed from office by 1560 and he died in 1561, so he could not have commanded in the Garha Katanga operation four years later.

question: Akbar's capture of Chittor in 1567-68 was significant because it:
option_1: Forced the complete surrender of Maharana Pratap
option_2: Marked the first Mughal victory over the Marathas
option_3: Gave Akbar control over Gujarat's ports
option_4: Defeated the Sisodia ruler Uday Singh and broke the resistance of the fort
solution_text:
The correct answer is Defeated the Sisodia ruler Uday Singh and broke the resistance of the fort.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In 1567-68 Akbar besieged and captured Chittor from Uday Singh of the Sisodia dynasty, breaking the main fort's resistance (चित्तौड़ की घेराबंदी — सिसोदिया शासक उदय सिंह के विरुद्ध)

 

• The fall showed that Akbar could crush even the proudest Rajput stronghold if it refused his authority.

 

• Maharana Pratap, Uday Singh's son, continued the struggle from the hills and fought at Haldighati in 1576.

 

• Resistance at Chittor was led by heroes such as Jaimal and Fatta.

 

• For the Mughals the capture of the hill fort also showed the value of siege techniques with mines and covered approaches, which Akbar used again at Ranthambore in 1569.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ranthambore was taken in 1569 after Chittor.

 

• Gujarat was annexed in 1572.

 

• Akbar's Rajput policy combined conciliation with force against defiant rulers.

 

• The Sisodias were ultimately conquered in Jahangir's time.

 

• The fall of Chittor was followed by the loss of Ranthambore in 1569 and Kalinjar in the same year, so Akbar took the three strongest Rajput forts in a short span.

 

NOTE

 

• Forced the complete surrender of Maharana Pratap (Option 1): Pratap did not surrender after Chittor; he went on to fight at Haldighati in 1576 and kept up the struggle until his death, so no complete submission happened in 1568.

 

• Marked the first Mughal victory over the Marathas (Option 2): The Marathas rose to power only in the seventeenth century under Shivaji, long after Akbar's reign, so a victory over them in 1568 is chronologically impossible.

 

• Gave Akbar control over Gujarat's ports (Option 3): Gujarat was annexed separately in 1572 and Akbar's victory there led to the Buland Darwaza; the Chittor siege occurred years before and is unrelated to the Gujarat ports.

question: Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri was built to commemorate Akbar's victory over:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gujarat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Buland Darwaza, 176 feet high, was built to commemorate Akbar's victory over Gujarat in 1572 (बुलंद दरवाजा — गुजरात विजय की स्मृति, फतेहपुर सीकरी)

 

• After that conquest Akbar renamed Sikri as Fatehpur Sikri, the City of Victory.

 

• It is the gateway to the Jama Masjid there and is considered the most imposing gateway in the world.

 

• The complex lies about 36 km from Agra.

 

• The Buland Darwaza thus stands as a victory monument, and the date of the Gujarat conquest also fixes the period when Fatehpur Sikri received its name and became the working capital of the empire.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Fatehpur Sikri also contains Jodha Bai's palace and the Panch Mahal.

 

• The Panch Mahal is inspired by a Buddhist vihara.

 

• Akbar later shifted the capital to Lahore because of water shortage.

 

• Sulh-i-kul is inscribed in the Buland Darwaza in tradition.

 

• The Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri was built in 1571-72, and the Buland Darwaza is placed on its southern side in red and yellow sandstone with marble decoration.

 

NOTE

 

• Malwa (Option 1): Malwa was conquered in 1561 by Adham Khan against Baz Bahadur, far earlier than the Fatehpur Sikri complex, and no gateway commemorates it.

 

• Chittor (Option 2): Chittor was captured in 1567-68, before Fatehpur Sikri was even founded, so the Buland Darwaza cannot commemorate that siege.

 

• Bengal (Option 4): Bengal was brought under Mughal control later in Akbar's reign, while the Buland Darwaza is explicitly tied to the 1572 Gujarat victory in the standard accounts.

question:
Arrange the following steps in Akbar's religious policy in chronological order:

1. Construction of the Ibadat Khana

2. Abolition of jiziya

3. Promulgation of Din-i-Ilahi

4. Abolition of the pilgrim tax
solution_text:
The correct answer is 4-2-1-3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The pilgrim tax was abolished first, in 1563, along with the forced conversion of prisoners of war (तीर्थ-कर 1563 → जज़िया 1564 → इबादतखाना 1575 → दीन-ए-इलाही 1582)

 

• Jiziya was abolished next, in 1564.

 

• The Ibadat Khana was built at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575, first for Muslim scholars and later for all religions.

 

• Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi) was announced in 1582.

 

• The sequence shows Akbar moving from removing discriminatory taxes, to opening a forum for debate, and finally to proclaiming a faith of his own that never became a mass movement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The new faith had only about fifteen followers, Birbal among them.

 

• Akbar did not compel anyone to join it.

 

• Aurangzeb reimposed jiziya in 1679.

 

• Sulh-i-kul was the central principle of his religious policy.

 

• The Ibadat Khana sessions were held on Thursday evenings, and quarrels among the ulema led Akbar to issue a declaration of infallibility, the Mahzar, in 1579.

 

NOTE

 

• 2-4-1-3 (Option 1): This order puts jiziya abolition before the pilgrim tax, but the notes and standard sources place the pilgrim tax in 1563 and jiziya in 1564.

 

• 4-1-2-3 (Option 2): This places the Ibadat Khana before the abolition of jiziya, yet the House of Worship was built in 1575, long after the 1563-64 tax reforms.

 

• 1-4-2-3 (Option 3): This begins with the Ibadat Khana of 1575, even though both tax abolitions came about a decade earlier, so it misplaces the first event.

question:
Consider the following statements about Din-i-Ilahi:

1. It was also called Tauhid-i-Ilahi.

2. Akbar compelled his nobles to join it.

3. It fizzled out after Akbar's death.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Din-i-Ilahi (the Divine Faith) was also called Tauhid-i-Ilahi, introduced in 1582 (दीन-ए-इलाही — अकबर द्वारा 1582 में प्रवर्तित)

 

• Statement 2 is incorrect: Akbar did not compel anyone to join; even in his lifetime it had only about fifteen followers, including Birbal.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: the faith failed and was rejected after Akbar's death.

 

• It believed in one God and tried to combine the good points of all religions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ibadat Khana debates in 1575 preceded the Din-i-Ilahi.

 

• Birbal was the most prominent follower.

 

• Sulh-i-kul or peace with all was the broader guiding principle.

 

• Akbar also separated religion from politics.

 

• Din-i-Ilahi had an initiation rite, where the follower pledged to give up pride, and the emperor himself acted as the spiritual guide of the members.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 only (Option 1): Choosing statement 1 alone drops statement 3, which is accurate since the new faith fizzled out and was rejected after Akbar died.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Compulsion is false, so the pair of the second and third claims collapses; Akbar left entry voluntary, and only a handful of courtiers ever joined the Divine Faith.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Selecting all three includes the false claim of compulsion, which contradicts Akbar's policy of Sulh-i-kul and the voluntary nature of the Divine Faith.

question: Akbar's policy of Sulh-i-kul was based on the principle of:
option_3: Universal tolerance and peace with all
solution_text:
The correct answer is Universal tolerance and peace with all.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sulh-i-kul means peace with all, the centrepiece of Akbar's religious policy, based on universal tolerance and religious harmony (सुलह-ए-कुल — सबके साथ शांति)

 

• It advocated equal treatment of all subjects regardless of faith.

 

• It was reflected in measures such as abolishing the pilgrim tax and jiziya and holding interfaith debates at the Ibadat Khana.

 

• Akbar is described as the first Mughal ruler to separate religion from politics.

 

• Equal treatment of all subjects meant that offices and honours were open to Hindus and Muslims alike, which explains why Rajput generals and Hindu ministers rose high in Akbar's service.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Akbar issued Ilahi coins of the Ram-Sita type in 1583.

 

• Persian became the official language of administration under him.

 

• Abul Fazal was the ideological spokesman of the policy.

 

• His reign is called the golden period of literature.

 

• Abul Fazal gave the philosophy of Sulh-i-kul its theoretical shape, which made it the guiding idea of the ruler towards all communities.

 

NOTE

 

• Military conquest (Option 1): Military conquest was a tool of Akbar's expansion but it is not the meaning of Sulh-i-kul, which concerns religious and social harmony among subjects.

 

• Religious exclusivity (Option 2): Religious exclusivity is the opposite of the idea; Akbar invited Hindus, Jains, Christians and others to debate and refused to privilege one faith.

 

• Strict Islamic orthodoxy (Option 4): Strict Islamic orthodoxy contradicts Akbar's inclusive attitude, which led him to end discriminatory taxes on non-Muslims and embrace many traditions.

question:
Match the Navratna of Akbar with their descriptions.

Column A: (a) Birbal (b) Todar Mal (c) Tansen (d) Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana

Column B: (i) Real name Mahesh Das (ii) Finance minister who gave the Zabti revenue arrangement (iii) Court musician who created Raj Darbari (iv) Son of Bairam Khan and a poet
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Birbal was originally Mahesh Das, a poet and singer given the title Raja by Akbar, so (a)-(i) (अकबर के नवरत्न — बीरबल, टोडरमल, तानसेन, रहीम)

 

• Todar Mal was the finance minister (Diwan-i-Kohi) whose revenue arrangement is the Zabti or Todarmal Bandobast, so (b)-(ii).

 

• Tansen, born Ramtanu Pandey, was court musician who created the raga Raj Darbari in Akbar's honour, so (c)-(iii).

 

• Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana was Bairam Khan's son and a poet, so (d)-(iv).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tansen earlier served Raja Ramachandra of Rewa.

 

• Rahim translated Bhaskaracharya's Lilavati into Persian.

 

• Abul Fazal and Faizi were brothers and also Navratna.

 

• Man Singh was the chief general among the nine.

 

• The group is a part of the Mughal court tradition and is a later grouping of nine famous courtiers of Akbar, among whom Birbal, Todar Mal, Tansen and Rahim were the best known.

 

NOTE

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv (Option 1): This reverses Birbal and Todar Mal, but Todar Mal handled finance and revenue while Mahesh Das is the real name of Birbal, so the first two pairings are wrong.

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iv, d-iii (Option 3): This exchanges Tansen and Rahim, yet Tansen is the musician and Rahim is the poet son of Bairam Khan; these descriptions cannot be swapped.

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 4): This assigns the Mahesh Das identity and the Raj Darbari creation to the wrong persons, as the singer Tansen and the poet Birbal are mismatched with the other entries.
